findings.topic: Royal submission, emigration, and patriotic symbols
findings.source_grounded_note: Artois’s departure, royal Paris visit, recognition of Bailly/Lafayette, and acceptance of the cockade visibly ratify lost royal initiative. The tricolour develops from city colours and Bourbon white.

Killings of de Launay, Flesselles, Foulon, and Bertier accompany suspicion of starvation plots. Barnave’s response differs from broad educated horror; Lafayette’s attempted resignation exposes the new Guard’s weakness.

Committees and militias supplant or monitor old municipalities under dual fear of popular disorder and royal revenge. Lawyers and newly active businessmen seek grain and order, while noble/clerical offers meet distrust.

findings.topic: Great Fear and pre-emptive rural action
findings.source_grounded_note: Subsistence insecurity, vagrancy, grain buying, conspiracy rumours, and news of royal defeat produce armed panic. Bands mistaken for brigands spread fear; anticipated law legitimates refusal and attacks in peasant understanding.

findings.topic: Destruction of feudal documentation and Quincey
findings.source_grounded_note: Attacks select dues records, seigneurial monopolies, and symbols rather than usually indiscriminate loot. Coerced renunciations and the Quincey explosion’s spreading interpretation intensify violence.

Breton Club tactics, d’Aiguillon, Noailles, and Le Chapelier begin with public-order aims; the session expands into fiscal/civil equality, abolished privileges and venality, clerical income changes, and open employment. Altruism coexists with settlement of old scores.

findings.topic: Abolition in law versus peasant destruction of feudalism
findings.source_grounded_note: The decree makes most dues redeemable and payable pending compensation; peasants’ refusal makes that settlement ineffective. Tithes disappear outright, while church lands temporarily remain. Harvest work and perceived vindication calm the countryside.

Abolition of binding mandates frees deputies to dismantle provincial, municipal, and occupational privileges beyond electoral instructions. Representative national sovereignty enables reconstruction without reconsultation.

findings.topic: Declaration of Rights and rule of law
findings.source_grounded_note: National sovereignty, general-will law, equal rights, liberty/property/security/resistance, due process, accountable officials, merit, equitable taxation, and separated powers form distinct usable routes; the declaration becomes foundational beyond its provisional intent.
reader_routes: Declaration of Rights of Man and Citizen

findings.source_grounded_note: Clerical resistance constrains religious-liberty language; thought/expression are protected subject to legally defined abuse and public order. Duties are mostly implicit, despite earlier drafts.

Mounier, Malouet, Lally-Tollendal, Clermont-Tonnerre, and Mirabeau favour British-inspired balance. A senate fails amid mistrust of peers and reopening legislative division; suspensive veto defeats both unlimited and no-veto positions.

findings.topic: Radical press and popular hostility to veto
findings.source_grounded_note: Saint-Huruge’s attempted march, Marat’s new paper, calls to purge deputies, and lamp-post threats show public pressure distinct from Assembly majorities and fear spreading beyond actual opponents.

findings.topic: October Days: subsistence, rumour, and coercion
findings.source_grounded_note: Dry rivers/mills prolong scarcity despite good crops; women’s action combines bread demands with cockade outrage and fear of troops. Royal assent precedes further palace violence and forced relocation; Lafayette follows pressure from his men and crowds.

Royal and Assembly relocation makes national institutions vulnerable to recurring Parisian intervention. Mounier warns of popular despotism, emigration expands, and open royal resistance to reform ends.

Legislative review, restricted veto, civil list, impeachment, and separation from ministers inhibit revived despotism. Suspicion of Mirabeau’s ambitions helps entrench exclusion of deputies from government.

Tax, sex, age, elector, and silver-mark thresholds distinguish political access from declared civil equality. Desmoulins challenges exclusion of the men who took the Bastille; election also supplies local, judicial, and clerical authority.

Abolition of parlements/venality/fees produces peace justices, district civil courts, departmental criminal courts, cassation, and juries. Courts lose administrative roles; public-order enforcement belongs to local authorities and Guard.

Eighty-three departments, districts, and communes replace inherited diversity. Elected underpaid officials supply implementation without central appointees, creating problems of capacity, experience, and sympathy. Map caption supports this broad organization, not an exhaustive map-name inventory.

findings.topic: Paris districts, sections, and Danton’s organization
findings.source_grounded_note: New sections aim to weaken old district radicalism, but the Cordeliers machine survives in Théâtre-Français. Newspapers and organization preserve wider political influence; map/section-key names alone are navigation rather than independent treatment.

Distrust of royal army makes Guard the approved coercive force. Martial Law authorizes fire after refusal to disperse; active-citizen membership, self-funded uniform, oaths, and officer restrictions aim at reliability.
Regional Guard rallies culminate in July 1790 oath-taking with king and Lafayette; Talleyrand’s mass and Ça ira express optimism at a high point of consensus, qualified by continuing dissent.

findings.topic: Noble alienation and persistent rural resistance
findings.source_grounded_note: Emigration, withdrawal from office, abolished nobility, and popular suspicion coexist with patriotic nobles. Refusal of legally retained dues, title destruction, Mays/liberty trees, and Guard participation in crowds defeat enforcement.

Destroyed collection machinery and intimidation become entrenched evasion; Babeuf organizes Picard protest. Assembly replaces indirect levies, monopolies, tax farms, and old direct taxes with land, movables, and commercial taxes, expecting willing payment without coercive machinery.

findings.topic: Debt honouring, failed loans, and Necker’s decline
findings.source_grounded_note: Commitment to honour national debt survives collapse in receipts. Failed loans, weak Patriotic Contribution, expanding compensation obligations, and damaged political standing undermine Necker’s authority.

findings.topic: Nationalization of Church property and contested ownership
findings.source_grounded_note: Talleyrand’s allocation proposal differs from Mirabeau’s general national disposal. Trusteeship/order extinction arguments conflict with institutional property rights; fiscal necessity, reform convictions, gallery anticlericalism, and predicted loyal buyers support confiscation.

findings.topic: Bank proposal, Law’s memory, and assignats
findings.source_grounded_note: Necker’s nationalized Discount Bank meets fear of paper collapse and rivalry between displaced Catholic financiers and Swiss/Protestant bankers. Mirabeau favours visible land-backed state bonds and Extraordinary Fund.

findings.topic: Assignats become money and a patriotic test
findings.source_grounded_note: Initial interest-bearing large bonds become legal tender, smaller denominations, and repeatedly enlarged issues as deficits/compensation grow. Political identification with the Revolution overrides Necker’s caution and precedes his resignation.

Cahiers broadly support constitutional monarchy, representation, equality, and liberty, but many specific institutions/abolitions have weak or no mandates. Innovation responds to events while retaining broad first-year support across social orders.

uncertainties.note: The supplied source states 3 November for acceptance of the Church-property motion; this review preserves the supplied date without external correction.
Maps were visually inspected. Caption descriptions are eligible; graphical details and navigational key do not independently establish substantive subjects under the frozen scope policy.

Page 122 places Lafayette’s forced march after the women’s October 5 arrival; page 126 says his men forced him to march on October 4 and associates the Flanders Regiment’s joining with that date. Preserve rather than silently harmonize these chronologies.
